claim: Gallego and van Ryzin (1994): when there is enough time to sell all items at the run-out price (lambda* t >= n), a fixed price p0 is guaranteed at least 97.5% of the optimal state-dependent expected revenue with 400 items, 95% with 100 items and 90% with 25 items (a bound from Theorem 3 for a known demand function, not a measurement).
note: Narrowed after refute A18: the 97.5, 95 and 90 percent figures hold only when lambda* t >= n; the general bound is 1 - 1/(2 sqrt(min{n, lambda* t})).

claim: Gallego and van Ryzin (1994) call their 97.5%, 95% and 90% guarantees quite pessimistic and say the fixed-price heuristic is good down to about 10 items.
Gallego and van Ryzin (1994): 'simple, fixed price policies are asymptotically optimal as the volume of expected sales tends to infinity' (a limit result, large expected sales).

Gallego and van Ryzin (1994): the fixed-price results hold only when the firm 'knows the demand function in advance and can price each instance of the problem (e.g., day/flight/voyage) individually'; with a shifting demand function a set of prices must be synthesised.
note: Narrowed after refute A19: the second condition (pricing each instance on its own) added.

claim: Gallego and van Ryzin (1994), Theorem 3: the fixed-price revenue ratio to the optimum is at least 1 - 1/(2 sqrt(min{n, lambda* t})), symbols as printed.
note: Symbols as printed; the text read is garbled in places.

claim: Talluri and van Ryzin (1998): bid-price control is not optimal in general, but when leg capacities and sales volumes are large it is asymptotically optimal, provided the right bid prices are used.
Talluri and van Ryzin (1998): a product is sold only if the offered fare exceeds the sum of the threshold prices of all the resources it needs.
Talluri and van Ryzin (1998): the bid prices are constant over time, even when demand is nonstationary, and may not be unique.

Talluri and van Ryzin (1998): in actual applications the approximation of the value function is usually re-solved frequently, so that bid prices adjust to remaining capacity and remaining time (a practice remark, no number, no industry named; the deterministic linear programme is one of the schemes examined).

Badanidiyuru, Kleinberg and Slivkins (2013): regret of O(sqrt(m OPT) + OPT sqrt(m/B)) up to logarithmic factors against the optimal dynamic policy, with m arms and B the smallest budget (form as printed).
Badanidiyuru, Kleinberg and Slivkins (2013): their regret bound is 'optimal up to polylogarithmic factors'.

Badanidiyuru, Kleinberg and Slivkins (2013): 'the process stops at the first time when the total consumption of some resource exceeds its budget', with time as one of the resources and a known finite horizon.
Badanidiyuru, Kleinberg and Slivkins (2013): per-round time is O(md) in the paper's notation.
Badanidiyuru, Kleinberg and Slivkins (2013): the optimal dynamic policy 'may significantly outperform the policy that plays the optimal fixed arm'.
Badanidiyuru, Kleinberg and Slivkins (2013): assumed that observations for a fixed arm 'are independent samples from a fixed joint distribution'.

Devanur, Jain, Sivan and Wilkens (2011): knowing only the number of requests m and not the distribution, Algorithm 2 gets a 1 - O(epsilon) fraction of the profit of the offline optimum W_E on the expected instance, with probability at least 1 - delta, for epsilon >= 1/m; epsilon approaches 0 only when no single request consumes a significant share of the global consumption.
note: Narrowed after refute A26: condition epsilon >= 1/m and the probability statement added (Theorem 2.2, paper.txt 452-460).

claim: Devanur, Jain, Sivan and Wilkens (2011), Theorem 2.2: for epsilon >= 1/m the guarantee W_E(1 - O(epsilon)) with probability at least 1 - delta assumes gamma = O(epsilon^2 / log(n/delta)), gamma being the largest share any one request takes of any capacity or contributes to W_E.
note: Narrowed after refute A26. Printed formula is garbled in the text read; its constants are not in the text read.

claim: Devanur, Jain, Sivan and Wilkens (2011): the algorithm 'does not require any knowledge of the distribution at all'.
Devanur, Jain, Sivan and Wilkens (2011): 'The algorithm knows m, the total number of requests'.

Devanur, Jain, Sivan and Wilkens (2011), Theorem 2.3: a nearly matching lower bound: there are instances where no algorithm, even with complete knowledge of the distribution, can get a 1 - o(epsilon) factor, so the trade-off cannot be improved much.
Agrawal and Devanur (2015), introduction only: the Devanur et al. (2011) algorithm 'is used in practice', but the actual problem has aspects that are not captured.
Agrawal and Devanur (2015), introduction only: the new algorithms 'achieve near-optimal regret guarantees for both the i.i.d. and the random permutation models'.
note: Summary-level: introduction only; not a full result.

claim: Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (2008): both their algorithms have competitive ratio ln(U/L) + 1, the deterministic one robust against any adaptive adversary.
note: Authors' report version from an archived copy, truncated; not the published WINE text.

claim: Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (2008): the competitive ratio of any online algorithm for the online knapsack problem is at least ln(U/L) + 1.
Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (2008): without their two assumptions 'there can be no online algorithm achieving any non-trivial competitive ratio'.
Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (2008): with several choices per step (multiple-choice knapsack) the ratio is '(ln(U/L) + 2)', Theorem 5.1.
Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (2008): with the largest item a share epsilon0 of the budget, the ratio is 'ln(Ue/L) / (1 - epsilon0)'.

Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (2008), abstract: with sniping and parameter tuning, the bidding algorithms 'can achieve a performance ratio above 90%' against the omniscient bidder, on synthetic data and real bid data gathered by hand.
note: The abstract's claim; the experiment tables were not read, so it is not checked against a table.

claim: Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (2008): in one simulation read, the unmodified strategy kept 'around 45%' of the omniscient bidder's value, 67% after the end-of-horizon price rise, and 'spends only 64% of the budget'.
note: The file is cut off inside section 6.1; this is the one simulation read.

claim: Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (2008) assume each item has weight much smaller than the knapsack capacity, 'w(t) << B'.
Zhou, Chakrabarty and Lukose (2008) assume the value-to-weight ratio lies between known bounds L and U.

Talluri and van Ryzin (1998), Management Science version: 'we accept a request for a particular itinerary if and only if there is available capacity and the fare exceeds the sum of the bid prices for all the units of capacity used by the itinerary'.
Talluri and van Ryzin (1998), Proposition 2: bid prices are optimal only if the opportunity cost of the itinerary equals 'the sum of the opportunity costs of selling each leg i separately'.
note: Formulas garbled in the text read.

claim: Talluri and van Ryzin (1998), Theorem 1: the revenue of the fixed-bid-price heuristic over the optimal revenue is '1 - O(u^-1/2)', tending to 1 as the problem is scaled up by u.
